extract:
Genesis formed in 1967 at Charterhouse, the English public school in Godalming, Surrey, when members of two student bands, the Garden Wall and the Anon, merged. The founding core of Peter Gabriel, Tony Banks, Mike Rutherford and Anthony Phillips began as a songwriting collective sending demos to Charterhouse alumnus Jonathan King. King named the group, signed them to Decca, and produced their debut, From Genesis to Revelation (1969), a set of orchestrated, Bee Gees-influenced pop songs that sold poorly. The band would remain active, in various line-ups, until their final concert in London in March 2022.

After parting with King, the group turned toward longer, more ambitious compositions shaped by hymnody, English folk and classical music. They signed with Tony Stratton-Smith's Charisma Records and released Trespass (1970), produced by John Anthony, whose closing track The Knife became an early stage favourite. Phillips left soon after, and drummer Phil Collins and guitarist Steve Hackett joined. This classic line-up made Nursery Cryme (1971), with The Musical Box, and Foxtrot (1972), whose 23-minute Supper's Ready became a cornerstone of progressive rock. Gabriel's theatrical performances, with costumes, masks and spoken storytelling, made the band a major live draw, as documented on Genesis Live (1973). Selling England by the Pound (1973) gave them their first UK hit single, I Know What I Like (In Your Wardrobe), and included Firth of Fifth. The double concept album The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway (1974) followed the Puerto Rican youth Rael through a surreal New York.

Gabriel left in 1975, and after auditioning many singers the band promoted Collins to lead vocalist. A Trick of the Tail (1976), co-produced with David Hentschel, kept the band's audience and showed Collins was a capable frontman. Wind & Wuthering (1976) continued in a pastoral, keyboard-rich vein. On tour, drummers Bill Bruford and later Chester Thompson filled in behind the kit, with guitarist Daryl Stuermer joining from 1978. Hackett departed after the live album Seconds Out (1977), and the remaining trio titled their next record And Then There Were Three (1978). Its single Follow You Follow Me gave them a transatlantic hit and signalled a move toward tighter songwriting.

The 1980s brought a decisive commercial shift. Duke (1980), featuring Turn It On Again and Misunderstanding, topped the UK chart. Abacab (1981), recorded at the band's own studio, The Farm in Surrey, with engineer-producer Hugh Padgham, stripped back their sound and added Earth, Wind & Fire's horn section on No Reply at All. Three Sides Live (1982) captured this era on stage. Later albums, including Genesis (1983), Invisible Touch (1986) and We Can't Dance (1991), made them one of the biggest-selling acts in the world, running alongside Collins's and Rutherford's (Mike + the Mechanics) parallel successes and Gabriel's acclaimed solo career.

Critical opinion has long been split between champions of the Gabriel-era progressive records and those who prefer the pop-oriented Collins years. Yet both phases proved influential. Neo-progressive bands such as Marillion drew heavily on the early catalogue, and tribute acts like The Musical Box recreate the 1970s stage shows. The band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2010. Banks, Rutherford and Collins reunited for the 2007 Turn It On Again tour and the 2021-22 The Last Domino? tour, with Collins's son Nic on drums, closing the band's performing life at London's O2 Arena.
title: Genesis
